name: Susanna Wesley
title: Susanna Wesley: teaching the faith in a house full of life
description: Susanna Wesley’s education, her influence on John and Charles, and the gatherings at Epworth show the reach of everyday service.

sections.heading: A woman who learned to think
paragraphs: Susanna Annesley was born in London in 1669. Her father, a Dissenting minister, encouraged a broad education for his daughters. Reading and examining ideas were part of her upbringing. Later, as Susanna Wesley, she held convictions of her own within a demanding family life.

She married Samuel Wesley in 1688, and the family settled in Epworth in 1697. They had nineteen children, ten of whom reached adulthood. The story of that household includes losses, financial hardship, and marital tensions that the memory of her famous sons should not hide.

sections.heading: Teaching around a table
paragraphs: Susanna gave importance to educating both her sons and her daughters. While Samuel was away in 1712, she gathered relatives and neighbors at the rectory for religious instruction. The Epworth museum documents these gatherings and the controversy they caused.

John and Charles Wesley received a lasting influence from their mother. That relationship helps explain part of their later path. It also lets us recognize a work of teaching carried out before the Methodist movement existed and within the daily responsibilities of a home.

reflection: In 2 Timothy 1:5 and 3:14–15, Paul recalls the faith Timothy came to know in his family and his learning of the Scriptures. Teaching can begin with a shared reading, a question that is listened to, and consistency in how we treat one another each day. It is a service that deserves time and the support of the community.

Susanna’s life does not offer a formula for raising children who will follow a particular path. Each person answers to God, and families go through different circumstances. We can value her attention to the education of girls and look with discernment at the discipline practices of her time.
review_note: The popular story of the apron as a place of prayer is avoided, since it is not confirmed in the source consulted. Historical discipline is not put forward as a universal model for raising children.
source_labels: Epworth Old Rectory. “Susanna Wesley,” profile from the Wesley family museum.
